title: Cocaine
why_this_matters: Cocaine toxicosis is infrequently suspected in dogs, and neurological signs predominate with frequent cardiovascular effects [1].

what_changes_from_human.point: Neurological signs predominate, but cardiovascular signs are frequent, and seizures, hypertensive crisis and tachyarrhythmia are possible [1].

recognition: In 19 dogs with a positive urine cocaine test, all had neurological abnormalities: bilateral mydriasis (58%), hyperexcitability or hyperesthesia (53%), ataxia (42%), tremors (42%), reduced mental awareness (32%) and seizures (16%) [1].
Tachycardia occurred in 53%, hypertension in 21% and hyperthermia in 26%. Sinus tachycardia was the only arrhythmia reported. Hyperglycemia (21%) and raised lactate (47%) were found [1].
management: 16 of 19 dogs were hospitalized for supportive care: isotonic fluids and sedatives or anxiolytics (diazepam, midazolam, acepromazine, chlorpromazine). Two needed further anticonvulsants and one an esmolol infusion [1].
All 19 survived to discharge, with a median stay of 15 hours. The authors recommend hospitalization for monitoring because of the potential for seizures, hypertensive crisis and tachyarrhythmia [1].
The series is limited to dogs with a positive urine cocaine test and comes from one hospital [1].

takeaway: A dog with dilated pupils, agitation, tremors and a fast heart rate may have taken cocaine; monitor and hand off to a veterinarian who can watch for seizures and hypertension.

sources.citation: Thomas E et al. 2014. Presumptive cocaine toxicosis in 19 dogs: 2004-2012. J Vet Emerg Crit Care.
